text:
Recent work separates factual support from personalized relevance. *On the Factual Consistency of Text-based Explainable Recommendation Models* (2025; revised 2026) evaluates atomic explanatory statements: high semantic similarity can coexist with poor factual precision. Its review-derived evidence is unavailable in this task, but claim-level verification remains applicable. [PURE (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03080) additionally distinguishes factual correctness from preference alignment; neither item accuracy nor historical association alone establishes why a particular user wants something. [Factual-consistency paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24366).

Evidence annotation offers useful safeguards. [GenAudit (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12566) links factual checking to supporting source passages. [AuRED (2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.arabicnlp-1.3.pdf) distinguishes supporting, refuting and insufficient evidence, with double annotation and Cohen’s κ. A separate [2024 annotation study](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.393/) pilots guidelines, discusses ambiguities, revises definitions and reports Krippendorff’s α. These support evidence-linked judgments and explicit abstention, rather than treating missing evidence as contradiction.

For this task, a proposed adaptation—not an established taxonomy—is to annotate broad association, documented compatibility/incompatibility, redundancy and insufficient information separately. Require exact title/description excerpts and explicit feedback quotations, recording their provenance. Compatibility needs documented specifications; redundancy needs identifiable duplication or explicit feedback. Missing specifications warrant abstention, never inferred incompatibility; histories alone cannot establish mood or dislike. Independently double-code the twenty users’ cases, report agreement before adjudication, preserve disagreements and abstention counts, and present category-level counts with denominators. With five users per category, findings describe observed failures rather than population preferences or causal explanations of validation HR@10.
